 The wind on the Isle of Skye did not merely blow; it screamed, a constant, ragged chorus that had been my only companion for thirty years. I was Elias Thorne, keeper of the Black Rock Lighthouse, a man whose life had shrunk to the size of the glass lens above me. My days were measured in the rotation of the beam and the ebb and flow of the tide, a rhythmic monotony that had long since worn away my curiosity, leaving behind only a hollow, echoing silence.

It was during the storm of November 12th, when the sea rose like a black mountain against the cliffs, that the letter arrived. It was not delivered by the supply boat, which had been delayed by three days of gale-force winds. Instead, it lay on the stone floor of the watch room, dry and pristine, as if it had materialized from the mist itself. The envelope was made of a paper so thin it seemed translucent, bearing no postmark, only my name written in an ink that shimmered with a faint, iridescent blue.

My hands trembled as I broke the seal. Inside was a single sheet of paper, the font crisp and modern, yet undeniably familiar. It read:

*Dear Elias,*

*You are wondering how this got here. Do not worry about the physics; worry about the choice.*

*In your timeline, you save the *Elara* on the night of the Great Gale. You see her lights struggling in the dark, and despite the exhaustion, you climb the stairs. You adjust the prism manually, overriding the automatic mechanism because you know the gear is slipping. You save forty-two souls. They live. They build families. They forget your name, but they remember the light.*

*But there is a cost. In saving them, you break your back. The cold seeps into your bones. By the time the rescue ship arrives, you are half-frozen. You survive, but the lighthouse becomes a prison. You spend the next twenty years watching ships pass by, never again feeling the thrill of the save. You become a ghost in your own life, haunting the tower until the day the automation replaces you entirely.*

*The alternative: Let the *Elara* go. Trust the automatic system. It is reliable. Most nights, it works. But tonight, the gear slips. If you do not intervene, the *Elara* hits the rocks. Forty-two lives lost. The village mourns. You are blamed, though it is not your fault. You leave the island. You move to the city. You paint. You love. You die at eighty, surrounded by art and laughter, your hands stained with oil paint rather than salt water.*

*Which life do you want, Elias? The hero who fades, or the artist who lives?*

*— From the Future*

I stared at the words, the rain hammering against the windowpane. Outside, through the swirling fog, I saw it. A flicker of orange light, distant and desperate. The *Elara*. Her engine was failing, her hull groaning under the weight of the waves. The automatic prism whirred overhead, steady and indifferent.

I looked at my hands, rough and cracked from decades of maintenance. I thought of the quiet dignity of the tower, the safety of routine. Then I thought of the city, of colors I had never dared to mix, of a life unburdened by the weight of other people’s survival.
